sections.sectionText: Experiments are performed on aqueous corrosion, sensitization of stainless steel, performance of Pb-free (Sn-Bi) solders, and failure analysis (on tractor parts provided by CATERPILLAR). The course emphasizes failure analysis and alloy design, the proper use of instrumentation (scanning electron microscopy, energy dispersive analysis, x-ray diffraction, mechanical testing, electrodynamic polarization testing of corrosion), communication skills, and respect for the importance of safety.

sections.sectionText: Exploration of emerging materials of reduced dimensionality through hands-on experiments. Students learn to handle/process atomically thin materials such as graphene, fabricate field-effect transistors from these materials, and carry out various means of characterization including electrical, Raman, and optical measurements. In addition, effects of external stimuli (e.g., mechanical and chemical) on electrical characteristics are also examined.

sections.sectionText: Students are introduced to emerging photovoltaic materials through hands-on experiments. Students fabricate and characterize solar cells made of materials such as organometal halide perovskites. Different methods to synthesize/deposit these materials and device architectures are examined. Students then critically examine advantages and challenges associated with integrating new materials into photovoltaics.

sections.sectionText: The course will provide fundamental principles and cover practical applications of the modeling of thermodynamics and kinetics in hard materials, including diffusion in binary and multicomponent alloys, nucleation and precipitation, spinodal decomposition, ordering, and solidification. Applications to practical situations and engineering materials will be developed using the commercial software Thermo-Calc and open-source continuum-scale (phase-field) modeling. This course does not require any coding. Prerequisites: MSE 401 and MSE 402 or equivalent courses or instructor approval.

sections.sectionText: Quantum technology can change the way we communicate, compute, and probe the natural world. Unfortunately, these applications are often hampered by issues related to materials science- defects, surfaces, heterostructures, film growth, fabrication, and beyond. In this class, students will learn the basics of qubits, coherence, quantum control and the different physical platforms utilized in quantum science. The connections between quantum and materials science will be explored through the examination of modern literature. Students will apply materials science techniques and principles to the outstanding problems in quantum information science in the form of projects and presentations.

restrictions: Restricted to Graduate - Urbana-Champaign.
sections.sectionText: Meets with ME 598 (48380) and CSE 498 (70543). We introduce the connection of materials and data science, and specific issues regarding experimental and computational materials data. Topics include data acquisition and management, data curation, uncertainty quantification, and applying machine learning to materials data. The focus will be on current scientific literature in the emerging materials and data area.

restrictions: Restricted to Graduate - Urbana-Champaign.
sections.sectionText: MSE 598 equips students with the experimental and analytical toolkit needed to characterize the structure of soft and biological materials across length scales spanning ångströms to micrometers. Through systematic study of the major technique families — X-ray scattering, electron cryo-microscopy, and atomic force microscopy — students develop the ability to select the appropriate technique for a given structural problem, design rigorous experiments, and critically interpret results. The course is structured to mirror how researchers actually work: grounded in technique fundamentals, then built toward integration. Practice problems and critical analysis of published literature train students to engage with real experimental data, and closing case studies drawn from soft matter and biological systems challenge students to synthesize complementary structural information across techniques. Students who take this course will be better prepared to design and execute characterization strategies in their own research and to interpret the primary literature with greater depth and confidence.
